societies.name: Black Mirror — San Junipero’s permanent residents
societies.society: Active human uploads living permanently in San Junipero

scope.period: The functioning permanent afterlife, including Yorkie and Kelly’s reunion
exclusions: Living trial visitors as permanent uploads
Dead people who were never uploaded

societies.description:
San Junipero supports active human continuations inside a computer-generated environment after their biological lives end. Ordinary bodily needs are supplied through the platform rather than through residents farming or earning a physical wage. This is a continuing place to live, not merely a recording replayed to relatives. The material-guarantee estimate is moderately strong for admitted permanent residents, but the checked story does not explain the full funding contract or an enforceable promise of indefinite server operation.

TCKR operates the hardware, so choosing an era or a personal experience is not the same as owning productive infrastructure. Control remains near the concentrated human-institutional side, with uncertainty about resident rights. The leisure-oriented setting supports a high nonworking estimate, explicitly a broad editorial judgment rather than a census. It allows substantial room for residents who choose useful creative or service activity. Living visitors have time limits and continuing physical needs; those different conditions are excluded from this permanent-person scope.

guarantees.basis: Permanent active life and automatic virtual support are realized, but funding, continuation rights and full admission rules are incompletely specified.

control.basis: The company hosts the environment; personal virtual choice does not establish ownership of the supporting hardware.

nonworking.basis: A recreational permanent afterlife strongly suggests high leisure; this broad noncanonical estimate allows many residents to undertake useful chosen work. The depicted couple is not a statistical sample.

evidence.claim: Human-derived permanent residents live actively in a recreational simulated environment hosted on TCKR hardware.
evidence.locator: Permanent-afterlife plot reveal/reunion and final server identification

uncertainties: Participation is a broad interpretive estimate, not a canonical census.
Permanent residents and living visitors have distinct material needs.
The company’s full financial contract remains unverified.
No unverified free-public-service or universal monopoly claim is made.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

societies.name: Love, Death & Robots — Sunset City’s robot retirement services
societies.work: Love, Death & Robots: Automated Customer Service
societies.society: Human retirees dependent on household and community robots

scope.period: Established retirement services through the featured customer’s lethal service failure
scope.population: Living human residents of Sunset City
exclusions: The dog as a human resident
All people in the outside economy
The original prose story as identical policy

societies.description:
Sunset City is an established retirement community where robots perform most routine work. The machines provide continuing domestic services rather than just a proposed convenience, weakening the need for residents to do the menial labor of everyday life. The record remains a narrow service-supported enclave: its financing and admission rules are not a universal income system. The guarantee estimate is weak because a provider can respond to a lethal malfunction by trying to sell protection instead of reliably stopping the danger.

Effective control stays near concentrated private service provision. Ownership of a household device does not give its customer dependable authority over the wider robot network, yet automated customer support alone does not prove that an independent AI owns the whole economy. A high nonworking estimate fits a retirement community with most routine tasks outsourced, but is deliberately broad. Care, gardening, art and other useful chosen activity can continue, so retirement is not scored as complete inactivity. One customer’s flight does not establish a new post-crisis society.

guarantees.basis: Routine support is real but contractual coverage is unclear and the provider offers paid protection from its own lethal devices; the single failure limits generalization.

control.basis: Customer requests do not reliably command the service network; the checked account does not establish autonomous AI ownership of the whole system.

nonworking.basis: Retirement and extensive menial-task replacement support a high broad estimate, with room for substantial useful voluntary activity; no exact census is claimed.

evidence.claim: An established retirement community uses robots for most routine work, while the featured provider tries to monetize protection during a lethal failure.

uncertainties: A robot-served retirement enclave, not a universal world economy.
The failure is not projected as identical suffering for every resident.
All estimates are provisional and participation is explicitly noncanonical.
Original story and animation are not automatically given identical media/economics.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

review_notes: Twelve short-check decisions, two service/virtual-life records, and broad explicitly noncanonical participation estimates where the setting gives a clear high-leisure direction.
No whole fiction read. Unrelated recipe hits were discarded; only exact White Christmas references are used.
Common People is not promoted merely because it automates one medical function; Whipple’s is a workplace rather than a whole support economy.
San Junipero funding assumptions are not invented. Sunset City’s single lethal failure qualifies security without assigning it identically to every resident.
